title: Beacons in the fog
subtitle: DNS rhythm, address ranges, and which way the bytes went
intro: Every ten minutes since 19:40, AUTOMATION-01 has asked the same question of DNS and made the same small connection. That rhythm is a scheduled task talking to whoever owns 203.0.113.44. Network events carry direction: principal is the side that started it, target is the side that answered. Read them that way and the night's traffic tells its own story.
concepts: CIDR notation names a range of addresses
Parentheses decide what OR applies to
sent_bytes is from the principal's point of view
recap: Recognise a fixed interval in a count as a beacon, not a person, and read it by the hour with by 1h
Read sent and received bytes together to tell a page load from a form post from a check-in
Test an IP field against a CIDR range with net.ip_in_range_cidr
Wrap an OR in parentheses, or use the grouped field ip, so either end of the wire is one condition
Compare bytes as numbers and read the direction from the principal's side

missions.title: The same question every ten minutes
missions.beat: Count DNS lookups for anything under the lookalike domain, grouped by the machine asking. One number will stand out.
missions.question: Which machine keeps looking up the lookalike domain, and how often?

concept.title: Regular intervals are a signature
concept.text: People browse in bursts. Scheduled code is punctual. Divide a machine's lookup count by the hours it spans: if it comes out to one every ten minutes, you are looking at the PledgeSync task's /mo 10 interval, not a person refreshing a page.

explain.meaning: Anchored to the end, so cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example and the bare domain both match.
How many lookup events each machine produced.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = /pier9-partners\.example$/
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = /pier9-partners\.example$/
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $lookups = count(metadata.id)
hints: Run it. Two machines appear; compare their counts.
Change match to principal.hostname, network.dns.questions.name to see which exact name each machine asked for.
AUTOMATION-01 made 62 lookups for cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example. PLEDGE-DESK-02 made one, at 18:52, for the bare domain.

answer.prompt: How many lookups did AUTOMATION-01 make?

call.prompt: Open the AUTOMATION-01 row's lookups: they are spaced ten minutes apart from 19:40 until nearly 06:00. What is the strongest reading?

options.label: A user kept refreshing the sponsor page all night from the playout PC, which has a browser like any other
A DNS misconfiguration on the playout PC is retrying a name it cannot resolve, once per cache expiry
Automated check-ins from the scheduled task: a beacon that outlived every human on shift

call.why: The spacing matches the task's /mo 10 interval exactly, and the lookups continue long after every human went home.

missions.clue: AUTOMATION-01 called home 62 times. PLEDGE-DESK-02 called once, at 18:52, when Hal followed the link. Two different stories from the same domain: one click, then one machine on a leash.

logIt.prompt: Log the cadence as evidence. Time: 19:40 to 05:50. Observation: AUTOMATION-01 looked up cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example 62 times, ten minutes apart, from 19:40:05 to 05:50:06; PLEDGE-DESK-02 looked the domain up once, at 18:52. Records: the first and last lookups. Write 'ten-minute cadence' in the observation, not 'beacon'; beacon is the hypothesis.

missions.caveat: Beacons in the wild add jitter and rotate names. A clean ten-minute cadence is a teaching case, not a promise.

missions.title: A page load and a form post
missions.beat: Before the rhythm, the click. Hal's desk made two connections to 203.0.113.44 within seventy seconds of resolving the lookalike. Read their byte counts in both directions and work out which was the page arriving and which was the password leaving.
missions.question: What do the two PLEDGE-DESK-02 connections to the attacker address look like, byte for byte?

concept.title: Direction is in the numbers
concept.text: A browser loading a page sends a small request and receives a large response: sent small, received large. Submitting a form sends the form and gets back a short acknowledgement or redirect: sent larger than received. Two connections, seconds apart, with the ratio flipped between them, is what a login page followed by a login attempt looks like from the outside of the encryption.

explain.meaning: Hal's desk talking to the attacker address. Nothing else on the pier did until 19:40.
From the principal's point of view: what the desk sent, what it got back. Compare the two rows.

hints: Run it. Two rows. Open each and read network.sent_bytes and network.received_bytes.
In the first row the desk received far more than it sent. In the second, the ratio is reversed.
18:52:31: sent 1,840, received 22,310 (a page arriving). 18:53:40: sent 2,210, received 1,180 (a form leaving).

answer.prompt: How many bytes did the second connection send (network.sent_bytes)?

call.prompt: Two connections: the first received twelve times what it sent, the second sent almost twice what it received. What does the pair show, and what does it not?

options.label: It shows a page was loaded and something was submitted a minute later; it does not show what was typed, which stays a hypothesis
It shows the pledge-desk password was entered on the fake portal; the byte sizes are the proof the brief has been waiting for
It shows nothing, because HTTPS hides the content and byte counts from a flow sensor are too noisy to read a direction from

call.why: Sizes and direction are readable through encryption and they fit a login form exactly. The content is not readable, so the password is inferred from what happened next, not observed here.

missions.clue: Page in at 18:52:31, form out at 18:53:40. Thirteen minutes later the guessing starts from outside and ends in a success. Nobody saw the password leave. Everything around that minute says it did.

logIt.prompt: Add a Timeline entry. Time: 18:53. Fact: PLEDGE-DESK-02 sent 2,210 bytes to 203.0.113.44 and received 1,180 at 18:53:40, seventy seconds after a connection that received 22,310 and sent 1,840; the shape of a page load followed by a form post. Evidence ref: the # of your click evidence (it carries the DNS lookup and at least one of these connections).

missions.caveat: A real login page loads scripts, images and fonts over several connections. The two-row version here is the shape stripped to its direction; expect dozens of rows in a real proxy log.

missions.title: Connections into the attacker's range
missions.beat: The lookalike resolves to 203.0.113.44. Attackers rarely own one address; they rent a block. Search for connections into the whole /24 on the web port.
missions.question: How many connections went to 203.0.113.0/24 on port 443?

concept.title: CIDR names a range
concept.text: 203.0.113.0/24 means 'the first 24 bits are fixed': every address from 203.0.113.0 to 203.0.113.255. net.ip_in_range_cidr tests an IP field against that range, so you catch neighbours of the one address you already know.

explain.meaning: A function used as a condition. First argument is the IP field, second is the range as a quoted string.
Numbers are unquoted. Port 443 is HTTPS, which hides the content but not the destination.

hints: The connections go to the attacker, so the attacker's address is on the target side.
The first argument is target.ip.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
net.ip_in_range_cidr(target.ip, "203.0.113.0/24")
target.port = 443

call.prompt: Every connection in your result used port 443. Does HTTPS make them safer?

options.label: No; encryption hides the content from you too, so destination, timing and volume are your evidence
Yes; encrypted traffic cannot carry stolen data out without breaking the TLS session, which the gateway would log
Yes; port 443 is allowed by the firewall, so whatever used it was approved traffic and is out of scope

call.why: Attackers use 443 because it is allowed everywhere and inspected nowhere. The metadata around the connection is what you can still read.

missions.clue: Sixty-five connections into the range: 63 from AUTOMATION-01, two from PLEDGE-DESK-02 at 18:52 and 18:53. The two from Hal's desk are the page load and the form post. Everything after that is the playout PC.

logIt.prompt: Log a Hypothesis, status supported: 203.0.113.0/24 is attacker infrastructure. The lookalike resolves into it, AUTOMATION-01 connects into it every ten minutes, and PLEDGE-DESK-02's two connections at 18:52 and 18:53 were the lure page and the form post. Supporting refs: your evidence entries for the click and the cadence. Supported means you cite them.

missions.caveat: The range here is from RFC 5737 documentation space and belongs to nobody. Never put a real indicator from work into a public trainer.

missions.title: Small both ways
missions.beat: Beacons are the opposite of a download. The task checks in, says almost nothing, hears almost nothing back, and sleeps. Pull every connection to the attacker address that sent less than a thousand bytes and look at what came back.
missions.question: How many of the connections to 203.0.113.44 are small enough to be check-ins?

concept.title: received_bytes and sent_bytes together name the pattern
concept.text: A page load receives much more than it sends. An upload sends much more than it receives. A beacon does neither: a few hundred bytes out, a few hundred back, over and over. Reading both fields on the same row tells you which of the three you are looking at. A numeric comparison on sent_bytes is how you cut the heartbeats away from the one connection that was not one.

explain.meaning: A numeric comparison. Bytes are plain numbers; no quotes.
Open a row: a few hundred bytes back each time. Compare with the 18:52 page load, which received over twenty thousand.

hints: You want connections that sent fewer bytes than the threshold. The operator is a comparison, not an equals.
Fill the gap with < so the line reads network.sent_bytes < 1000.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
target.ip = "203.0.113.44"
network.sent_bytes < 1000

call.prompt: Every small connection sent between about 820 and 980 bytes and received between about 380 and 460. Three connections to the same address fall outside the cut. What are they?

options.label: Retries of failed beacons, which send more because they include the queued check-ins the task could not deliver earlier
The two connections from Hal's desk at 18:52 and 18:53, and the 48 MB upload from the playout PC at 02:10
Noise from the sensor: flow logs occasionally merge two beacons into one record, which doubles the byte counts

call.why: Sixty-two heartbeats, all alike. The three that are not alike are the three moments that mattered: the page, the form and the theft.

missions.clue: Sixty-two connections under a thousand bytes out, each a few hundred back, ten minutes apart from 19:40 to 05:50. Sixty-five to the address in all. The other three are the click, the form and the upload.

logIt.prompt: Log the beacon shape as evidence. Time: 19:40 to 05:50. Observation: 62 NETWORK_CONNECTION events from AUTOMATION-01 to 203.0.113.44:443 each sent under 1,000 bytes and received a few hundred; the remaining three connections to that address are the two from PLEDGE-DESK-02 and the 48 MB upload. Records: the first small connection (open it, press Add to Casebook). Write the sizes; "beacon" stays the hypothesis.

missions.caveat: Real beacons vary their size and timing on purpose. Thresholds found on one night are a starting point for a rule, not the rule.

missions.title: Either end of the wire
missions.beat: Hal's workstation is 10.9.4.22. Odalys wants everything it talked to and everything that talked to it. Direction matters, so you have to ask about both roles.
missions.question: How many connections involved 10.9.4.22 in either role?

concept.title: Parentheses decide what OR applies to
concept.text: AND binds tighter than OR. Without parentheses, A AND B OR C reads as (A AND B) OR C, which would drag in every event where C is true regardless of type. Wrap the OR so it is one condition.

explain.meaning: Either role may hold the address. The parentheses keep both alternatives inside the event-type filter.
ip = "10.9.4.22" does the same job in one token. Both forms pass here because they return the same evidence.

hints: Either alternative may be true, so the word between them is OR, not AND.
Fill the gap with OR and keep the parentheses.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
(principal.ip = "10.9.4.22" OR target.ip = "10.9.4.22")

call.prompt: You drop the parentheses and the count jumps to hundreds. What happened?

options.label: Search ignored the OR and treated the three conditions as one long AND, matching far more than intended
The query became (type AND principal) OR target, so every event with that target IP, of any type, was added
The grouped field ip was triggered by the repeated address and matched both roles at once across every event type

call.why: Operator precedence silently changed the question. The results looked plausible, which is the dangerous part.

missions.clue: Twenty-one connections. Nineteen are the evening's ordinary browsing and mail. Two are the 18:52 and 18:53 connections to 203.0.113.44 that followed the phishing link. Hal's machine is a victim's machine, not the attacker's.

logIt.prompt: Add a Timeline entry. Time: 18:52. Fact: PLEDGE-DESK-02 (10.9.4.22, hal.brunner) resolved pier9-partners.example and connected to 203.0.113.44 twice; its other 19 connections tonight are ordinary browsing and mail. Evidence ref: the # of your click evidence. A timeline entry points at evidence; it never stands alone.

missions.caveat: principal.ip and target.ip are repeated fields in real UDM. This trainer models one value each; the docs cover how repeated values and negation interact.

missions.title: Either end, in one token
missions.beat: The streaming CDN at 192.0.2.120 is what the playout PC listens to all night, and other desks reach it too. Odalys wants every connection that touched it, either as the side that started it or the side that answered. Last mission you wrote the OR by hand; this time use the grouped field ip.
missions.question: How many connection events involved 192.0.2.120 in either role?

concept.title: A grouped field is an OR you did not have to write
concept.text: ip = "192.0.2.120" expands to principal.ip = "192.0.2.120" OR target.ip = "192.0.2.120", parentheses included. One token, no precedence trap. The price is speed: the engine checks every member field. Use the grouped form when you genuinely do not know which side the address sits on, and the explicit field when you do.

explain.meaning: Google's grouped field for addresses. Covers principal.ip and target.ip in this dataset.
The hand-written equivalent from the last mission. Both forms pass here because they return the same evidence.

hints: The grouped field for addresses is two letters long and is listed in the About page's supported subset.
Fill the gap with ip, no dots, no role.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
ip = "192.0.2.120"

call.prompt: Your count for the CDN is higher than the 65 connections into the attacker range, and seven machines reached it. Does that make the CDN the bigger lead?

options.label: Yes; the address with the most connections from the most machines is where an analyst starts, and the attacker range can wait
No; every machine on the pier streams from it, the bytes flow inward, and that is what a shared service looks like, which is why it is the baseline and not the lead
Neither; both addresses are on port 443 and the counts are close enough that only a reputation feed can rank them

call.why: Breadth is what benign infrastructure looks like: many machines, many connections, data coming in. The attacker address had two machines, data going out, and a clock.

missions.clue: Seventy-four connections touched the CDN, from seven machines, data flowing in. Sixty-five touched the attacker address, from two machines, data flowing out on one of them. The grouped field asked the same question either way; the shape of the answer is what differs.

logIt.prompt: Write a Harden item: give AUTOMATION-01 an egress allowlist of the services it needs (the streaming CDN at 192.0.2.120 and the vendor update host) and alert on any new destination. Answers: your cadence evidence and your beacon-shape evidence. Owner role: network engineer. Urgency: this week.

missions.caveat: Google's grouped ip field spans more members than the two modelled here, and its behaviour with negation and repeated fields is documented separately. Read that page before you rely on != with a grouped field.

missions.title: Beacons by the hour
missions.beat: Sixty-two is a total. The board will ask whether it ever stopped. Count the connections from the playout PC to the attacker address in one-hour buckets and read the rhythm as a table.
missions.question: Across how many clock hours did the playout PC check in with the attacker address?

concept.title: by 1h puts the clock in the grouping key
concept.text: A match section can group by a field and by a time window at once: by 1h adds one row per hour, fixed on the clock. A regular task shows up as the same number in every full hour; a break in the rhythm, or an hour with one connection too many, is a row that reads differently from its neighbours. Read down the column, not across it.

missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
target.ip = "203.0.113.44"
match:
  principal.hostname by 1h
outcome:
  $beacons = count(metadata.id)
hints: Filter to connections from AUTOMATION-01 to 203.0.113.44, then group by the hostname with a one-hour window, and count.

match:
  principal.hostname by 1h
outcome:
  $beacons = count(metadata.id) under the three filter lines.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
target.ip = "203.0.113.44"
match:
  principal.hostname by 1h
outcome:
  $beacons = count(metadata.id)

answer.prompt: How many rows does the table have (hours with at least one connection)?

call.prompt: Every full hour shows six connections, the first hour two, and one hour shows seven. What is the seventh?

options.label: A retry after a dropped beacon; tasks on a ten-minute schedule occasionally fire twice when the previous run overlaps
The 02:10 upload: six heartbeats plus the one connection that carried the donor list, in the same hour, to the same address
A rounding effect of fixed clock buckets, which can put a 59-second connection into the next hour and inflate it

call.why: Six per hour is the ten-minute task. The hour with seven holds the one connection that was not a heartbeat; the bucket found it without anyone reading sizes.

missions.clue: Eleven hours, 19:00 to 05:00. Two in the first partial hour, then six, six, six, every hour until morning, except the 02:00 hour, which has seven. The rhythm never stopped. One beat in it was the theft.

logIt.prompt: Log a Hypothesis, status supported: the connections from AUTOMATION-01 to 203.0.113.44 are automated check-ins from the PledgeSync task, six per hour from 20:00 to 05:00 with no gap, and the 02:00 hour's seventh connection is the upload. Supporting refs: your cadence evidence and your beacon-shape evidence. Supported means you cite them.

missions.caveat: Google's match windows are fixed on the clock, as here. A burst that straddles an hour boundary is split across two rows; read neighbouring rows together.

missions.title: The one big upload
missions.beat: Beacons are small. Theft is not. Find any connection tonight that sent more than ten megabytes out. Bytes are plain numbers; compare them like numbers.
missions.question: Where did the large outbound transfer go?

concept.title: sent_bytes is from the principal's point of view
concept.text: network.sent_bytes counts what the principal transmitted to the target. A workstation that sends 48 MB to an outside address in one connection has uploaded something. Received bytes would mean a download. Read the direction before you say which.

hints: A numeric comparison: the sent-bytes field greater than ten million, written as a bare number.
network.sent_bytes > 10000000 with the connection event type.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
network.sent_bytes > 10000000

answer.prompt: What is the target.ip of the large transfer?

call.prompt: One connection: 48,230,112 bytes sent from AUTOMATION-01 to the attacker address at 02:10, five minutes after donors_export.zip was written. What can you state, and what remains inference?

options.label: State: the donor list was stolen at 02:10. The size, the timing and the file name together prove what the stream contained
State: nothing, since the connection was encrypted and the bytes cannot be read back from the log or the sensor
State: a 48 MB upload to the attacker address followed the zip. Inference: the zip's contents were the payload

call.why: You can prove the size, the direction, the destination and the timing. Proving what was inside the stream needs the file itself or the attacker's server, neither of which you have.

missions.clue: One connection over ten megabytes all night: 48 MB from the playout PC to 203.0.113.44 at 02:10:33. The pirate segment at 03:10 read donor names on air. The donor list left the building an hour before that. The broadcast was the announcement, not the theft.

logIt.prompt: Write a Contain item: block egress to 203.0.113.0/24 at the gateway and isolate AUTOMATION-01 from the network until it is rebuilt. Answers: your cadence evidence and your click evidence. Owner role: network engineer. Urgency: now. The 48 MB upload itself goes in the Evidence tab in the next mission.

missions.caveat: Byte counts depend on the sensor. Flow logs, proxies and EDR disagree by headers and retransmits. Treat a size as approximate and the direction as reliable.
